lesson.title: The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de
lesson.subtitle: Why French says 'some bread' (du pain, de la soupe) and collapses it to bare de after negation (pas de pain).

hook.title: Why French Never Leaves Mass Nouns Naked: du, de la, de l', des
hook.content: Where English says bare 'I want bread, soup, and water', French requires the Partitive Article (de + definite article = 'some'): du pain (de + le), de la soupe, de l'eau, des livres (de + les)! And when you negate the verb ('I don't want any bread'), the quantity drops to zero and all four collapse to bare de / d': Je ne veux pas de pain, Je n'ai pas d'eau!

footnotes.title: Why zero quantity collapses du / de la / des to bare de
footnotes.content: After ne...pas, ne...plus, ne...jamais, or quantity words (beaucoup de, un peu de, combien de), the definite article inside du/de la/des vanishes, leaving bare de!

pattern.title: Positive: du / de la / de l' / des → Negative: pas de / pas d'
pattern.content: Use du (m.), de la (f.), de l' (vowel), des (pl.) in positive sentences, and collapse them to de / d' after negation.
pattern.linguist_note: French is strictly determiner-obligatory; bare nouns cannot occupy argument positions.
pattern.trap_note: Never keep du/de la/des after pas (*Je ne veux pas du pain) — collapse to pas de pain!

exercises.prompt: Match each positive partitive phrase with its negative 'pas de' counterpart:

matching_pairs.english: Je veux du pain (some bread, m.)
matching_pairs.german: Je ne veux pas de pain

matching_pairs.english: Je prends de la soupe (some soup, f.)
matching_pairs.german: Je ne prends pas de soupe

exercises.target_answer: Je ne veux pas de pain, Je ne prends pas de soupe, Je n'ai pas d'eau, Je n'ai pas d'amis
exercises.meaning: Je veux du pain (some bread, m.), Je prends de la soupe (some soup, f.), J'ai de l'eau (some water, vowel), J'ai des amis (some friends, pl.)
exercises.explanation: du, de la, de l', and des all collapse to bare de (or d') after negation.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Je veux du pain et de l'eau'?
exercises.german: Je veux du pain et de l'eau
options: I want the bread and the water
I want of-the bread and of the water
exercises.target_answer: I want of-the bread and of the water
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I want of-the bread and of the water
exercises.explanation: du (de + le) and de l' literally mean 'of-the' ('some portion of the').

exercises.prompt: Flip 'Je veux du fromage' ('I want some cheese') into the negative ('I don't want any cheese'):
options: Je ne veux pas de fromage
Je ne veux pas du fromage
exercises.target_answer: Je ne veux pas de fromage
exercises.explanation: After ne...pas, partitive du collapses to bare de: pas de fromage!

exercises.idea: I want some bread and some cheese please
cues: I want some bread → Je veux du pain
and some cheese, please → et du fromage, s'il vous plaît
idea_parts: first partitive → Je veux du pain
second partitive + polite tag → et du fromage, s'il vous plaît
exercises.target_answer: Je veux du pain et du fromage, s'il vous plaît
exercises.meaning: I want some bread and cheese, please
exercises.explanation: Both pain and fromage take masculine partitive du.

diagnosis.cue: Use du pain et du fromage.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Je ne veux pas de vin ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Je ne veux pas de vin ce soir
exercises.meaning: I don't want any wine tonight
exercises.explanation: du vin collapses to de vin after ne...pas.
exercises.affirmation: You collapsed du to bare de after pas!

summary.outcome: Use partitive articles (du, de la, de l', des) for unspecified quantities and collapse them to bare de/d' after negation.

use_example.german: Je prends du pain et de la soupe, mais je ne prends pas de vin.
use_example.english: I'm having bread and soup, but I'm not having wine.

summary.takeaway: Use du / de la / de l' / des for 'some', and collapse to bare de after pas.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([14] Possessives Agree with the Thing): see how The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de leads directly into Possessives Agree with the Thing.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I want some bread and cheese, please" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je veux du pain et du fromage, s'il vous plaît
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je veux du pain et du fromage, s'il vous plaît" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de.

du.etymology_derivation: Does double duty: 'from the' (du train) and the masculine partitive 'some' (du pain, du café).

de.etymology_derivation: Latin dē 'down from' — of and from in one small word.

des.etymology_derivation: Plural of un/une: where English says bare 'books', French says des livres ('some books').

pain.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis 'bread' — a pantry is literally the bread-room. The N is thought, not said: the nasal vowel is the lesson.

vin.context_translation: I would like some red wine.

fromage.etymology_derivation: Latin caseus formāticus ('cheese made in a form/mold') — French kept the mold word!

soupe.etymology_derivation: Takes feminine partitive de la: de la soupe.

eau.shift_rule: Latin aqua, all three vowels are ghosts of a
eau.etymology_derivation: Latin aqua → ea → eau: one syllable wearing two vowels and a consonant as historical scar tissue. Feminine: l'eau.

pas.etymology_derivation: negation grew from ne vais pas un pas — 'I don't go a step'. Pas is literally a footstep, the same word as pace.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.
